audits.claim: §6: 'Tone is not exotic: ~42% of WALS languages lack it, ~33% simple tone, ~25% complex.'
audits.source_locator: WALS Online ch. 13 'Tone' (Maddieson 2013), section 2 'Definition and distribution of the categories'
audits.source_excerpt: "Of the 526 languages included in the data used for this chapter, 306 (58.2%) are classified as non-tonal." and "About a quarter of the languages (132, or 25.1%) have simple tone systems."
audits.basis: Retrieved percentages are 58.2% non-tonal / 25.1% simple / 16.7% complex (the chapter's Map 13A table lists 307/527). The entry's numbers match none of them. Only the '2-tone systems most common' clause is consistent (simple two-way 132 vs complex 88 among tone languages). Dated erratum appended to the entry (## Errata, 2026-10-17).
audits.access_limit: None (open access). WALS-internal discrepancy noted: prose 306/526 vs map table 307/527.

audits.claim: §2 WALS anchor: modal consonant class 19–25, ~35% of 562 languages (Maddieson 2013).
audits.source_locator: WALS Online ch. 1 'Consonant Inventories' (Maddieson 2013), section 1 and Map 1A value table
audits.source_excerpt: "The more typical consonant inventory size is in the low twenties, with the mean for the 562 languages being 22.7, the modal value 22 and the median 21."
audits.basis: Chapter defines 'average' as 22 ± 3, i.e. 19–25; the Map 1A table gives Average = 201 of 563 languages. 201/563 = 35.7% (~35%), a count computed from the retrieved table, not a percentage stated in the text. Mean 22.7 / modal 22 / median 21 quoted directly.
audits.access_limit: None (open access). Mean is over 562 languages while map categories total 563; the entry's '562' matches the mean's denominator.

audits.source_locator: WALS Online ch. 2 'Vowel Quality Inventories' (Maddieson 2013), section 2 and Map 2A value table
audits.source_excerpt: "Languages with “average” vowel quality inventory size account for more than half the total sample (51.2%)" and "Considerably more languages have an inventory of five vowels than any other number — 188 or just over one-third."
audits.basis: The 5–6 'average' category is 287 of 564 (50.9%, chapter prose 51.2%), not ~45%; five qualities alone are 188 (~33%). Modality of the 5–6 group holds; the figure does not. Dated erratum appended to the entry (## Errata, 2026-10-17).
audits.access_limit: None (open access). The chapter's 559-language correlation subsample differs from the map's 564 total; the 5–6 count is read from the map table.

audits.source_locator: WALS Online ch. 12 'Syllable Structure' (Maddieson 2013), section 3 and Map 12A value table
audits.source_excerpt: "By far the most common type are languages which permit moderately complex syllable structure, accounting for about 56.5% of the sample."
audits.basis: The retrieved sample is 486 languages, not 534; 'simple' is 61 (~12.5%) and the ~56% figure belongs to the 'moderately complex' category (CVC / limited CCV onsets). No retrieved Maddieson 2013 chapter carries a 534-language sample. Dated erratum appended to the entry (## Errata, 2026-10-17).
audits.access_limit: None (open access). Map 12A table total 486 (simple 61, moderately complex 274, complex 151); chapter prose says '150 languages (about 30.9%)' complex.

audits.claim: §7: the tone ↔ dry-climate (desiccation) association is contested; independent reanalysis fails to reproduce it (entry cites Roberts 2018 among the critiques).
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved_full_text (Frontiers HTML article; full body extracted, fetched 2026-10-17)
audits.source_excerpt: "Study 1 replicates a previous analysis of the link between humidity and lexical tone with an alternative dataset and finds that it is not robust."
audits.basis: Coupling audit (language × environment). The retrieved abstract also reports Study 2 finding 'no significant correlation' with a continuous tone measure, and Study 3 finding a robust but small humidity–vowel effect. This directly supports the entry's 'contested' calibration and its citation of Roberts (2018) as a failed replication.
audits.access_limit: None for this article (open access). The original Everett, Blasi & Roberts 2015 PNAS text was not retrieved (pnas.org HTTP 403); the other named critiques (Hammarström 2016; Collins 2016/2017; Donohue 2016; Hartmann et al. 2024) were not individually re-fetched.

audits.claim: §7: ejectives ↔ altitude (Everett 2013) — 'mechanism argued' half of the entry's calibration.
audits.source_excerpt: "We suggest that ejective sounds might be facilitated at higher elevations due to the associated decrease in ambient air pressure, which reduces the physiological effort required for the compression of air in the pharyngeal cavity"
audits.basis: Coupling audit (language × environment). The retrieved abstract documents the 567-location elevation/ejective correlation and two proposed motivations (reduced air pressure; mitigated water-vapor loss), matching the entry's 'mechanism argued'. The 'sampling criticized' half is audited separately as PHON-A07.
audits.access_limit: None (open access). The statistical models were not re-run; only the paper's own statements are cited.

audits.claim: §7: ejectives ↔ altitude — 'sampling criticized; not established' half of the entry's calibration.
audits.source_excerpt: "we do not find strong support for either a correlation of ejectives or uvulars with high-altitude environments, though the association is somewhat stronger for ejectives than uvulars … suggests a strong role of language contact rather than environmental factors"
audits.basis: Coupling audit (language × environment). An independent Bayesian/phylogenetic reanalysis contests the altitude–ejective link, supporting 'sampling criticized; not established'. The separately retrieved Maddieson & Benedict 2023 (Frontiers in Psychology 14:1200463) likewise says of this connection: 'This connection has been questioned by Urban and Moran (2021)', while itself confirming the raw correlation and doubting the water-vapor mechanism (aspirated stops are more likely at higher altitude).
audits.access_limit: None (open access). The Bayesian models and phylogenetic analyses were not re-run.

audits.claim: §7: whistled registers exist and reproduce a spoken language (Silbo Gomero as the entry's example).
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved_full_text (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage element page, fetched 2026-10-17)
audits.source_locator: UNESCO ICH, Silbo Gomero element description (inscribed 2009), body text
audits.source_excerpt: "The whistled language of La Gomera Island in the Canaries, the Silbo Gomero, replicates the islanders' habitual language (Castilian Spanish) with whistling." and "two distinct whistles replace the five Spanish vowels, and there are four whistles for consonants"
audits.basis: Coupling audit (language × environment / communication channel). Institutional source confirms a whistled register that re-encodes a spoken language with a reduced whistle inventory, and notes traditional transmission and ceremonial use.
audits.access_limit: The entry's mechanism clause (mountains + long-distance herding; Meyer 2008) is not addressed by this source and was not re-verified this round; the Kuşköy element page was not located (one wrong-URL probe returned a different UNESCO element and was discarded).

audits.claim: §7: 'though raw global correlations (Maddieson & Benedict 2023) … still fit' — the tone–humidity counterevidence clause.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved_full_text (Frontiers HTML article; full body extracted, fetched 2026-10-17)
audits.source_locator: Maddieson & Benedict 2023, Frontiers in Psychology 14:1200463, section 4.2 'Replications', Figure 11 discussion
audits.source_excerpt: "As for the proposed relationship between tone and higher humidity (Everett et al., 2015, 2016), we find an overall increase in the average humidity values with increasing complexity of tone systems (Figure 11)."
audits.basis: Coupling audit (language × environment). Authorship and venue confirmed from the article's own citation block ('Maddieson I and Benedict K (2023) … Front. Psychol. 14:1200463'), matching the entry's citation exactly. The paper reports the tone–humidity pattern across its own ~1,000-language database while stressing confounds and a 'broader framework of language types' — consistent with the entry's 'still fit… flavor, never law' framing.
audits.access_limit: None (open access). The paper's 'preliminary analyses' wording means this is an association, not a controlled causal result; the entry already flags the debate as contested.

audits.claim: §2 extremes: Rotokas is an inventory-size extreme (entry states 11 phonemes, Firchow & Firchow 1969).
audits.source_locator: WALS Online ch. 1 'Consonant Inventories' (Maddieson 2013), section 1, Rotokas sentence
audits.source_excerpt: "Rotokas (West Bougainville; Papua New Guinea) has only six consonants."
audits.basis: Independent typological database confirms Rotokas' extreme smallness with six consonants and notes the wide allophonic range behind the simplified /p t k b d g/. The entry's 11-phoneme total also requires 5 vowels per Firchow & Firchow 1969; the vowel half was not re-retrieved this round, so only the consonant half is confirmed here.
audits.access_limit: WALS gives the consonant count, not the entry's 11-phoneme total; Firchow & Firchow 1969 itself was not fetched.
